Canva

Higher Education at Canva

Universities buy Canva for Higher Education to give their whole campus access. The people who make that call usually work in IT, marketing or administration. But most visitors to the Higher Education page, about 60%, were actually faculty and students who don’t make the purchase. I redesigned the page to keep buyers on it, and created a new Faculty page so faculty had a home of their own.

Visual DesignProduct Design
Role
Product Designer
Team
Marketing Technology
Timeline
1 month
Tools
Figma, UserTesting
Business model
SaaS/Tech

The Challenge

  • Sending buyers away at peak intent

    The Contact Sales button took buyers to a separate page, right when they were ready to get in touch.

  • Nowhere for faculty to go

    Students had their own page, but faculty didn’t. They either left or filled in a sales form that wasn’t meant for them.

  • Mostly non-buyers

    About 60% of identified traffic was non-buyers, and the Student page was only mentioned in an unlinked line in the FAQ.

  • Relevance that took too long to land

    49% of visits didn’t scroll at all and 57% bounced. There was nothing aimed at specific buyers like IT or Marketing.

The Solution

Two pages that work together: a Higher Education page for buyers, and a new Faculty page for faculty.

  • Re-routing above the fold

    A module right at the top points faculty and students to their own pages.

  • A brand new page for faculty

    Students already had a page, and now faculty have one too.

  • Contacting sales is even easier

    The primary CTA is a jump link to an embedded form, so users aren’t redirected off the page.

  • Messages for each buyer persona

    Tabs for IT, Marketing, and Student & Academic Affairs, each with its own reasons to choose Canva.

The Benefits

  • Better leads for Sales

    Fewer non-buyers should reach the form, so Sales can focus on institutions ready to buy.

  • A page for every audience

    Faculty and students find content made just for them, instead of bouncing.

  • Less drop-off at peak intent

    Buyers can reach out without leaving the page that convinced them.

  • Faster relevance

    Each buyer finds what matters to them in one click.

Design decisions

  • Changing what success meant

    The original ask was more submissions, but the data showed the real issue was who was submitting. I proposed measuring lead quality instead, and agreed with stakeholders up front that fewer submissions could be a good result.

  • Questioning the data

    Analytics showed Enterprise visitors at about 1% of traffic. That’s likely too low, because a university IT manager wouldn’t call themselves “Enterprise”. So we measure the drop in non-buyers instead, which we can track reliably.

User testing

I ran an unmoderated usability test with the hifi designs with 5 participants:

  • All 5 understood who the page was for on first read
  • Participants went straight to the tab that matched their role
  • Buyers recognised the page was for them and not faculty or students

Experimentation

The redesign is being A/B tested 50/50 against the original page across English-speaking markets.

  • What we’re measuring

    Lead quality (MQLs) and Contact Sales submissions, with the qualified submission rate as a guardrail.

  • Questioning the data

    The original sent buyers to a separate form, while the redesign uses an embedded one, so we track the two separately for a fair comparison.

The Outcome

Both pages are live, and the A/B test is in progress. A big part of this project was deciding who the page wasn’t for, and making sure those visitors had somewhere better to go.
